author: reek
body: Pass 2 cannot run until pass 1 has finished the whole frame, and that is not an implementation detail: a reflection can land on a pixel far from the one being shaded, so any pixel of the image may be needed. Interleaving the passes would sample a half-drawn frame, which is the same failure the magenta clear was added to catch and would be much harder to see.

author: reek
body: The height-field march, again. `TerrainRender` has one and it cannot be cited, because it carries an `opening`; but this one is not the same traversal anyway. It has to resolve a lake plane against the ground and decide which of the two the ray met first, and the step cap is here for the reason recorded in that chapter -- the bracket must not hold two crossings.

author: reek
body: Where the ray meets the lake surface, if it does. A ray climbing away from the water never meets it.

author: reek
body: Nearest wins, with one guard: the lake only exists where the ground under it is lower than the water. On a scene this shape the guard is redundant, because ground standing above the lake plane would have stopped the ray before it got there, but it costs one height sample and it makes the rule explicit rather than a consequence.

author: reek
body: The water normal. Two crossed ripples, small enough to keep the surface readable as water rather than as a disturbed mirror. This is what makes the reflection wobble, and it is also what the roughness perturbation in the model acts on top of.

author: reek
body: A traced sample fills a 2x2 block, so reading the colour of traced pixel (tx,ty) means reading the framebuffer at twice those coordinates. Pass 2 samples through here, which is the moment the technique becomes literal: this reads the picture it is drawing.

author: reek
body: The reflection. Everything that makes SSR what it is happens in these twenty lines.

author: reek
body: The march starts a little way off the surface along the normal. Starting exactly on it means the first probe compares the surface against its own recorded depth and reports a hit immediately, and the water reflects itself -- a flat wash of water colour that looks almost plausible, which is what makes it worth naming.

author: reek
body: On a miss the sky stands in. A real implementation would fall back to a pre-rendered environment probe, and the sky IS that probe here; the fade toward the screen edge blends between them so the boundary does not draw a line across the water.

author: reek
body: The hit count is ACCUMULATED and not recorded in the G-buffer, and the first version of this got that wrong in a way worth keeping a note about. Marking each pixel's outcome back into the flag byte seemed a tidy way to count them, but pass 2 READS that same byte: every water pixel already processed carried its outcome instead of its material, so the self-reflection reject could never match and the buffer the march depends on was being rewritten underneath it, row by row, as the pass advanced. A pass that consumes a buffer must not also write it.

author: reek
body: A cheap decorrelated value per pixel, the same shape as the cloud model's jitter and for the same reason: neighbouring pixels must not perturb their reflection the same way, or the noise organises itself into bands.

author: reek
body: How much water is in frame, and how much of it found something to reflect. Both are printed, because a reflection pass that runs over zero water pixels and one that runs over thousands and misses every time produce the same image, and neither announces itself.

author: reek
body: Low over the water, and that is a physical decision rather than a compositional one. Fresnel governs how much a dielectric reflects, and for water it runs from about 0.02 head-on to nearly 1.0 at grazing incidence. A camera looking DOWN at a lake therefore sees almost no reflection, correctly: the first framing here sat 80 m above the surface and produced water that was accurately, uselessly dark. Dropping the eye to a few metres above the waterline is what puts the reflection where it can be seen, and it is also what a photographer would do.
